[0] Currently in charge of the temple's affairs, Ms. Ying (a pseudonym), a descendant of the Chow family, revealed to a photojournalist that years ago her Tanka fisherman grandfather had unexpectedly retrieved a wooden statue of "Fourth Sister" while out at sea. He brought the statue home and gave it to the young Ying as a toy, and she even sewed clothes for it. Unexpectedly, Ying subsequently fell ill with a high fever, and her grandmother was visited by "Seventh Sister" in a dream, instructing her grandfather to place the statue in a temple for worship. The Chow family obeyed this divine instruction and built the present-day Temple of Seventh Sister.

[1] The Temple of Seventh Sister is renowned for the efficacy of prayers for romance, and Ying shared a romantic anecdote. One evening on the sixth day of the seventh lunar month three years ago, a slightly chubby man with a touch of "baby fat" waited patiently in front of the temple until midnight of the seventh day to pay his respects, and returned to do the same the following year. Only yesterday evening on the sixth day, that same man, dressed in red, arrived hand in hand with his girlfriend to fulfil his vow. Ying initially did not recognise him, until he took his girlfriend's hand and smiled sheepishly at Ying, allowing her to identify the lovelorn devotee and bear witness to their blossoming romance.

[2] When it comes to insights on worshipping at the Temple of Seventh Sister, Ying believes it is simply about communicating with the deities: "Say whatever is on your mind, tell Seventh Sister your worries." Like having a "chat," if one wishes to know Seventh Sister's advice and the outcome, one may cast divination blocks. During the Qixi Festival, the Temple of Seventh Sister is not only a sacred place for seeking blessings of romance, but also a haven where devotees can pour out their hearts.
